{{Short description|Point not touching any other point}}
{{Other uses|Glossary of tables game terms#closed point}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''closed point''' of a [[topological space]] is a [[point (geometry)|point]] whose [[singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] is [[closed set|closed]]. In many areas of [[geometry]] and [[topology]], all spaces under consideration are [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> spaces]] that only have closed points. The distinction between closed and non-closed points is most often made in [[algebraic geometry]], where [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] can have non-closed points.

==Definition and motivation==
If <math>X</math> is a [[topological space]], a point <math>x \in X</math> is called '''closed''' if the singleton <math>\{x\}</math> is [[closed set|closed]].<ref name="Vakil121">{{harvnb|Vakil|2025|p=121}}</ref> An equivalent statement is that the [[closure (topology)|closure]] <math>\overline{\{x\}}</math> only contains <math>x</math>.

The closed points of a space <math>X</math> can also be defined using the [[specialization preorder]] on <math>X</math>. Given points <math>x,y \in X</math>, <math>x</math> specializes to <math>y</math> if <math>y \in \overline{\{x\}}</math>. This means that the closed points of a topological space are those that specialize to no point except themselves, that is, the [[maximal and minimal elements|most specific]] points.{{efn |There is no general agreement on whether "more specific" should be regarded as lower or higher.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|pp=213,428}}</ref> Depending on this, the closed points can be either minimal,<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|pp=93–94}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Johnstone|1986|p=66}}</ref> or maximal.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=103}}</ref>}}

Spaces where every point is closed, called [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> spaces]], are common.<ref name="DST4">{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=4}}</ref> In most branches of mathematics, it is rare to encounter spaces that have any non-closed points. Many mathematicians regard such spaces as somewhat strange. For example, if <math>x</math> specializes to <math>y</math>, the [[constant sequence]] <math>(x,x,x,...)</math> [[limit (mathematics)|converges]] to <math>y</math> (as well as <math>x</math>).<ref>{{harvnb|Munkres|2000|p=98}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Schechter|1996|p=439}}</ref>

In [[algebraic geometry]], [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] usually have many non-closed points, including points whose closure <math>\overline{\{x\}}</math> is rather large. In particular, every [[irreducible component]] of a scheme <math>X</math> is of the form <math>\overline{\{x\}}</math> for some <math>x \in X</math>. This can make the study of schemes easier since some properties of <math>x</math> extend to the entirety of <math>\overline{\{x\}}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|pp=77–78}}</ref>

==Examples==
[[Image:SpecZ original.png|right|300px|thumb|The spectrum of '''[[integer|Z]]''', which is a [[principal ideal domain|PID]]. The generic point is depicted as a grey line that contains all other points.]]

* Most of the typical examples of spaces are [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], and in particular [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]].<ref>{{harvnb|Munkres|2000|p=99}}</ref> This includes [[manifold]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Munkres|2000|p=225}}</ref> Other examples of T<sub>1</sub> spaces include [[non-Hausdorff manifold]]s,<ref>{{harvnb|Gauld|2014|pp=153–154}}</ref> [[algebraic varieties]],<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|p=36}}</ref> and spaces with the [[cofinite topology]].<ref>{{harvnb|Schechter|1996|pp=107,440}}</ref>
* When an [[algebraic variety]] is considered as a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]], every [[Zariski topology|Zariski]]-closed [[subvariety (algebraic geometry)|subvariety]] of it is endowed with an additional point, which is [[generic point|generic]] in that subvariety. The original points of the variety are the closed points of the resulting scheme.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|pp=77–80}}</ref>
* In the [[spectrum of a ring|spectrum]] of a [[commutative ring]], the points are the [[prime ideal]]s of the ring, and the closed points are the [[maximal ideal]]s.<ref name="Vakil121"/>
* In particular, the points of the spectrum of a [[principal ideal domain]] are the ideals generated by [[prime element]]s (defined [[up to]] a [[unit (ring theory)|unit]]) and the [[zero ideal]]. The points that correspond to prime elements are closed, and the point that corresponds to zero is generic.<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|pp=46–47}}</ref>
* The [[Sierpiński space]] has two points. One of them is closed, and the other is non-closed since it specializes to the first point.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|pp=8–9}}</ref>
* The closed points of a [[partially ordered set]] with the [[Alexandrov topology#Correspondence with preordered sets|Alexandrov topology]] are the [[minimal element]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Viro|Ivanov|Netsvetaev|Kharlamov|2008|pp=39,40,326}}</ref>
* If two points are [[topologically indistinguishable]], the closure of either of them contains both and hence neither of them is closed.

==Properties==
In any scheme that is locally [[morphism of finite type|of finite type]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]], the set of closed points is [[dense set|dense]].<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2025|p=164}}</ref> In particular, this is true for schemes that correspond to algebraic varieties.<ref name="Vakil121"/> This is not always the case, even for an [[affine scheme]]. For example, the spectrum of a [[discrete valuation ring]] is (topologically) the aforementioned [[Sierpiński space]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|p=74}}</ref> Nonempty [[quasi-compact]] schemes (and in particular affine schemes) must have at least one closed point.<ref name="GW7892">{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|pp=78,92}}</ref> However, there are schemes without any closed points at all,<ref>{{harvnb|Vakil|2025|pp=436–437}}</ref> including [[irreducible scheme|irreducible]] schemes.<ref name="GW7892"/>

In any scheme that is locally of finite type over a field <math>k</math>, the [[residue field]] is [[finite extension|finite]] over <math>k</math> at closed points and [[transcendental extension|transcendental]] over <math>k</math> at non-closed points.<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|p=81}}</ref> In particular, if <math>k</math> is algebraically closed, the closed points are exactly those where the residue field is <math>k</math> itself.<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|p=83}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|p=81}}</ref> This implies that every <math>k</math>-[[rational point]] is closed, and if <math>k</math> is algebraically closed then the closed points are exactly the <math>k</math>-rational points.<ref>{{harvnb|Görtz|Wedhorn|2020|p=121}}</ref> In a scheme of finite type over <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, the closed points are exactly the points where the residue field is [[finite field|finite]], and each finite field is the residue field at only finitely many points. This makes it possible to define the [[arithmetic zeta function]] of such a scheme.<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|1965|p=83}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kahn|2020|pp=21–23}}</ref>

Let <math>X</math> be affine scheme (or equivalently, a [[spectral space]]). <math>X</math> is [[normal space|normal]] if and only if its closed points can be [[separated sets|separated by neighborhoods]].<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=281}}</ref> If the space of closed points of <math>X</math> is [[connected space|connected]], <math>X</math> is connected too, and the converse holds if <math>X</math> is normal.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=200}}</ref> If <math>X</math> is normal, the space of closed points of <math>X</math> is [[compact space|compact]] (and [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]).<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=283}}</ref> A normal affine scheme is simply the spectrum of a commutative [[Gelfand ring]],<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=246}}</ref> so these are in fact properties of the [[maximal spectrum|maximal spectra]] of such rings.

==Locally closed point==
A '''locally closed point''', or a '''Goldman point''', is a point <math>x \in X</math> such that the singleton <math>\{x\}</math> is [[locally closed subset|locally closed]]. This is equivalent to the condition that <math>x</math> is [[isolated point|isolated]] in <math>\overline{\{x\}}</math>. Every closed point is locally closed.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|p=135}}</ref>

Unlike the case of closed points, the locally closed points are dense in every affine scheme.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickmann|Schwartz|Tressl|2019|pp=132,139}}</ref>
